findings.description: The reports_archive bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so objects (including the vendor roster spreadsheet) are stored with only S3's default SSE-S3 or no enforced encryption, and no customer-managed KMS key protects the data at rest.
The ledger_exports bucket contains financial ledger data but declares no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving exported ledger objects unprotected by any configured encryption at rest.
The model_artifacts bucket configures versioning and logging but no server_side_encryption_configuration, so stored machine-learning artifacts are not encrypted with a specified key at rest.
The ops_runbooks bucket stores operational runbooks that commonly contain credentials and internal procedures, yet it defines no server_side_encryption_configuration for encryption at rest.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block / block_public_acls is attached to the reports_archive bucket, so account-level or bucket-policy settings could allow public exposure of archived reports.
The ledger_exports bucket relies on a private ACL alone and has no public access block, meaning a later ACL or bucket-policy change could silently expose ledger data publicly.
The model_artifacts bucket sets a private ACL but no S3 public access block, so nothing prevents the bucket or its objects from being made publicly readable.
The ops_runbooks bucket has no public access block configured, leaving sensitive runbook content potentially exposable via a future policy or ACL change.
Even the audit_trail bucket, which holds log data, has no public access block defined, so its contents could be exposed if bucket policy or ACLs are later loosened.

The audit_trail bucket uses acl = "log-delivery-write", which grants the S3 log-delivery group write and ACL-read permissions on the bucket; this broad grant is unnecessary with modern log-delivery mechanisms and expands the set of principals able to modify bucket contents.

Model artifact access logs are written to aws_s3_bucket.audit_trail without a target_prefix encryption guarantee; combined with the lack of a target object ownership/ACL restriction this can leave log objects readable by the log-delivery account.
